kcet|Chemistry|2005|13||0|0:
An emulsion is one liquid dispersed as droplets in another with which it does not mix, such as
oil in water. Left alone the droplets coalesce and the two layers separate, because the
interfacial tension between them is high.
An **emulsifier** (emulsifying agent) prevents that. Its molecules are amphipathic — one end
polar, the other non-polar — so they collect at the oil–water interface, the hydrophobic tail in
the oil and the hydrophilic head in the water.
This lowers the interfacial tension and forms a protective film round each droplet, keeping
them apart so the emulsion does not break. Soap, casein in milk and gum acacia all work this way.
(3) is the opposite of what it does — coagulating would destroy the emulsion.
(2) and (4) describe the mechanical act of mixing, not what the added substance achieves.
∴ it stabilises the emulsion.

kcet|Chemistry|2005|14||0|0.s:
**Transition metals** make the best catalysts, and their partly filled d orbitals are the reason.
Those d orbitals let them do two things.
First, they adsorb reactant molecules onto the surface using unpaired d electrons, weakening
the bonds within the reactant and lowering the activation energy — as nickel does with H₂ in
hydrogenation, and iron with N₂ in the Haber process.
Second, they show **variable oxidation states**, so they can give an electron and take it back
again, forming unstable intermediates that provide an alternative pathway. Vanadium cycling
between V(V) and V(IV) in the contact process is the standard example.
Alkali and alkaline earth metals have no partly filled d orbitals and only one stable oxidation
state, so they can do neither — which rules out (1), (2) and therefore (4).
∴ transition metals.

kcet|Chemistry|2005|16||0|0:
This is a basic buffer — a weak base with its salt — so use the Henderson–Hasselbalch
equation in the pOH form:
pOH = pKb + log([salt]/[base])
Equal volumes are mixed, so each concentration is **halved**:
[NH₄OH] = 0.2/2 = 0.1 M
[NH₄Cl] = 0.02/2 = 0.01 M
Substitute, with pKb = 5:
pOH = 5 + log(0.01/0.1)
= 5 + log(0.1)
= 5 + (−1)
= 4
pH = 14 − pOH = 14 − 4 = 10
The halving actually cancels out of the ratio, so the answer would be the same without it —
but it is worth doing, because in other buffer problems the absolute concentrations matter.
∴ pH = 10.

kcet|Chemistry|2005|17||0|0.s:
For the hydrogen electrode, H⁺ + e⁻ ⇒ ½H₂ with the gas at 1 atm, the Nernst equation reduces
to a very simple form.
E = E° − (2.303RT/F)·log(1/[H⁺])
E° = 0 by definition for the standard hydrogen electrode, and the bracket is given as 0.059 V:
E = −0.059 · log(1/[H⁺])
= +0.059 · log[H⁺]
= −0.059 · pH
So the electrode potential is just −0.059 times the pH. With pH = 3:
E = −0.059 × 3 = −0.177 V
The sign matters: in any solution more dilute in H⁺ than 1 M, the potential is negative.
Option (1) gives the right magnitude with the wrong sign, which is the usual slip.
∴ −0.177 V.

kcet|Chemistry|2005|18||0|0.s:
Work in milliequivalents, since the strengths are given as normality:
meq = volume (ml) × normality
meq of NaOH = 35 × 0.1 = 3.5
The hydrochloric acid supplied works out to more than this, so after neutralisation some acid
is **left over** and the resulting solution is acidic.
Now apply the indicators:
**Methyl orange** changes over pH 3.1–4.4 — red in acid, yellow in alkali. In an acidic solution
it turns **red** ✓
**Phenolphthalein** changes over pH 8.3–10 — colourless in acid, pink in alkali. With excess
acid it stays colourless, so option (3) is wrong.
The solution is therefore neither neutral (1) nor basic (2).
This is also why methyl orange, not phenolphthalein, is the indicator chosen for titrating a
strong acid against a weak base: it responds in the acidic range where that end point falls.
∴ it will turn methyl orange red.

kcet|Chemistry|2005|21||0|0.s:
A precipitate forms when the ionic product exceeds the solubility product:
[Ag⁺][Cl⁻] > Ksp = 10⁻¹⁰
The crucial step is that **equal volumes** are mixed, so every concentration is **halved**
before the comparison.
(1) 10⁻⁴ and 10⁻⁷ ⇒ (5×10⁻⁵)(5×10⁻⁸) = 2.5 × 10⁻¹² ✗
(2) 10⁻⁵ and 10⁻⁶ ⇒ (5×10⁻⁶)(5×10⁻⁷) = 2.5 × 10⁻¹² ✗
(4) 10⁻⁶ and 10⁻⁶ ⇒ (5×10⁻⁷)(5×10⁻⁷) = 2.5 × 10⁻¹³ ✗
(3) 10⁻⁵ and 10⁻⁴ ⇒ (5×10⁻⁶)(5×10⁻⁵) = 2.5 × 10⁻¹⁰ ✓ — greater than 10⁻¹⁰
Only the third exceeds Ksp, so only there does AgCl come out of solution.
Forgetting to halve would make option (1) appear to work (10⁻¹¹... still short) and would
wrongly admit others — the dilution on mixing is the point of the question.
∴ 10⁻⁵ M AgNO₃ and 10⁻⁴ M HCl.

kcet|Chemistry|2005|22||0|0:
Density is mass per unit volume, so a defect lowers the density only if it removes **matter**
from the crystal without changing its size.
**Schottky defect** — equal numbers of cations and anions are missing from their lattice sites
altogether, leaving vacancies. The volume of the unit cell is unchanged but its mass has
fallen, so the density **decreases** ✓ Shown by NaCl, KCl, CsCl and AgBr.
**Frenkel defect** (1) — an ion merely moves from its lattice site into an interstitial site. It is
still inside the crystal, so the mass is unchanged and so is the density.
**F-centres** (3) — an electron occupies an anion vacancy. An electron has negligible mass, so
the effect on density is imperceptible; what it changes is the colour.
**Interstitial defect** (4) — an extra particle is squeezed in, so the density actually **rises**.
Equal numbers of each ion must leave in a Schottky defect, or the crystal would not stay
electrically neutral.
∴ Schottky defect.

kcet|Chemistry|2005|23||0|0.s:
Work backwards from what is left now.
Number of half-lives in 40 days:
n = 40/10 = 4
Each half-life halves the amount, so going **backwards** in time each step **doubles** it:
125 mg ⇒ 250 ⇒ 500 ⇒ 1000 ⇒ 2000 mg
Or directly: original = 125 × 2⁴ = 125 × 16 = 2000 mg
Convert the units, since the options mix mg and g:
2000 mg = 2 g
That unit conversion is where the question catches people — option (2), 600 mg, and option (4),
1.5 g, are both there to catch an incomplete calculation.
Radioactive decay is first order, so the half-life stays 10 days throughout and the halvings
simply compound.
∴ 2 g.

kcet|Chemistry|2005|24||0|0.s:
A particle accelerator works by applying an electric or magnetic field, and a field can only
exert a force on something that carries **charge**.
Check the charges:
α-particle — a helium nucleus, charge +2 ✓ can be accelerated
β-particle — an electron, charge −1 ✓ can be accelerated
Proton — charge +1 ✓ can be accelerated
**Neutron** — electrically **neutral**, charge 0
With no charge, a neutron experiences no force in any electric or magnetic field, so it cannot
be accelerated by a cyclotron or any similar machine.
This is also why neutrons are such effective nuclear projectiles: nothing repels them, so even
a slow neutron can reach a nucleus, whereas a positively charged α-particle must overcome
the nuclear charge. Fast neutrons are produced by nuclear reactions instead, and slowed with
a moderator.
∴ neutrons.

kcet|Chemistry|2005|27||0|0:
In a blast furnace the coke serves two purposes, and the question is which does the actual
reduction.
The hot air blast first burns the coke to carbon dioxide, releasing heat, and the CO₂ is then
reduced by more coke to carbon monoxide:
C + O₂ ⇒ CO₂  then  CO₂ + C ⇒ 2CO
It is that **carbon monoxide**, rising through the charge, that reduces the iron oxide in the
cooler upper region at 400–700 °C:
Fe₂O₃ + 3CO ⇒ 2Fe + 3CO₂
Carbon itself (3) does reduce iron oxide, but only lower down where the temperature exceeds
about 1100 °C, and it is the minor route.
The hot air blast (1) supplies oxygen and heat but is an oxidising agent, not a reducing one,
and silica (4) is the flux, removing the gangue as slag.
∴ carbon monoxide.

kcet|Chemistry|2005|28||0|0.s:
An alloy is a homogeneous mixture of metals, and forming one requires the atoms to be
mutually soluble — similar in size, and compatible in crystal structure or chemical nature.
(1) Zn and Cu — similar atomic radii and both fcc; they dissolve in each other completely to
give brass ✓
(3) Fe and C — carbon is small enough to occupy the interstices of the iron lattice, giving the
interstitial alloy steel ✓
(4) Hg and Na — sodium dissolves readily in mercury to give sodium amalgam, used as a mild
reducing agent ✓
(2) **Fe and Hg** — iron is one of the very few metals that will **not** dissolve in mercury. It
forms no amalgam at all.
This is of real practical use: mercury can be stored and transported in **iron** containers
precisely because it does not attack them.
∴ Fe and Hg cannot form an alloy.

kcet|Chemistry|2005|29||0|0:
Work out the oxidation state of the metal in each complex. Remember that CO and NH₃ are
**neutral** ligands while CN⁻ and Cl⁻ carry −1.
(1) [Cu(NH₃)₄]SO₄ — the sulphate outside is 2−, so the complex ion is 2+. With four neutral
ammines, Cu = +2.
(2) [Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂] — neutral overall; two neutral ammines and two chlorides at −1 each give
Pt = +2.
(4) K₃[Fe(CN)₆] — three K⁺ outside, so the complex ion is 3−. Six cyanides at −1 total −6, so
Fe = +3.
(3) [Ni(CO)₄] — the complex is neutral and all four carbonyls are neutral, so
x + 4(0) = 0 ⇒ **x = 0**
Nickel is in the **zero** oxidation state ✓
That is characteristic of metal carbonyls, and it is possible because CO stabilises a low
oxidation state through synergic π back-bonding, accepting the excess electron density the
metal would otherwise carry.
∴ [Ni(CO)₄].

kcet|Chemistry|2005|30||0|0.s:
Alum, K₂SO₄·Al₂(SO₄)₃·24H₂O, purifies water by **coagulating** the suspended matter.
Muddy water carries clay and silt as a **negatively charged** colloidal sol; the like charges on
the particles repel one another, so they stay dispersed and never settle.
Dissolving alum releases Al³⁺ ions. By the Hardy–Schulze rule, a triply charged cation is an
extremely effective coagulant for a negative sol: it neutralises the charge on the particles,
the repulsion disappears, and they clump together into flocs heavy enough to settle out.
The Al³⁺ also hydrolyses to a gelatinous Al(OH)₃ precipitate, which sweeps further impurities
down with it as it falls.
It does **not** soften hard water (2) — alum adds ions rather than removing Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ —
and it neither flavours the water (3) nor kills bacteria (4), which is why chlorination is still
needed afterwards.
∴ because it coagulates the impurities.
